nameStory: The 'butterfly' in butterfly stonecrop comes from this plant's amazing ability to attract butterflies and other pollinators with its showy pink flower clusters. The 'stonecrop' part refers to the plant's remarkable ability to grow in rocky, harsh conditions where other plants struggle - it literally crops up among stones! This tough succulent earned its place in gardens worldwide for both its beauty and resilience.
description: Butterfly stonecrop is a sturdy, upright succulent plant that forms neat clumps about 18-24 inches tall and wide. It has thick, fleshy blue-green leaves that feel rubbery to the touch and store water like a cactus. In late summer, the plant tops itself with spectacular flat-topped clusters of tiny pink flowers that create a landing pad effect for visiting butterflies and bees. Though native to Asia, this popular garden plant occasionally escapes cultivation in New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, flat-topped clusters of tiny star-shaped pink flowers bloom in late summer, each flower having 5 petals and feeling papery when touched

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, succulent leaves that feel like rubber erasers, blue-green in color with slightly toothed edges and arranged alternately up the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms upright clumps 18-24 inches tall with multiple sturdy stems emerging from the base, maintaining its shape even in poor conditions

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, fleshy stems that feel firm and substantial, often with a reddish tinge, especially near the base

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Entire plant has a waxy, succulent feel - leaves and stems store water and feel cool and smooth to the touch

habitat: In New England, butterfly stonecrop is primarily found as an escaped garden plant near old homesites, stone walls, and disturbed areas with well-drained soil. It thrives in sunny spots with sandy or rocky soil and can tolerate drought conditions that would stress most other plants. Look for it in abandoned gardens, along roadsides, or in rocky areas where it has naturalized from nearby plantings.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as thick, blue-green shoots from the base, with leaves unfolding in compact rosettes that feel cool and rubbery.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full height with mature succulent foliage, building toward their spectacular late-summer flower display.
seasonality.fall: Peak bloom time with showy pink flower clusters buzzing with butterflies and bees, followed by brown seed heads that persist.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back to ground level, leaving only the hardy root system to survive New England's cold.

funFact: Butterfly stonecrop can survive being pulled from the ground and left without water for weeks - its leaves will actually continue to photosynthesize and the plant can re-root itself if given the chance, earning it the alternate name 'live-forever'!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other garden sedums, but butterfly stonecrop's large size, flat-topped pink flower clusters, and thick blue-green leaves set it apart from smaller, yellow-flowered relatives. Remember: if it's tall enough to look you in the eye and covered in pink flowers that butterflies love, it's likely butterfly stonecrop.
contextualKnowledge: This plant is sometimes still sold under its old scientific name Sedum spectabile, so don't be confused if you see it labeled that way in older garden books or nurseries. The genus was recently moved from Sedum to Hylotelephium based on genetic studies, but gardeners still often call the whole group 'sedums.'
compareHints: Butterfly stonecrop is larger and showier than its relatives, reaching 2 feet tall versus the 6-12 inches of most other stonecrops in New England. While orpine has similar succulent leaves, butterfly stonecrop's flowers are distinctly pink and arranged in flatter, broader clusters. The blue-green leaf color is also more pronounced than in other members of the live-forever genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Orpine differs from other stonecrops in its much larger size and robust growth habit - while most stonecrops are low, creeping plants, orpine stands tall and upright.
Pink Mongolian stonecrop differs from its New England relatives like orpine and garden stonecrop by its trailing, mat-forming habit and distinctive blue-gray leaves.
Garden stonecrop differs from its close relative orpine by having more distinctly spoon-shaped leaves and typically paler flowers.
Compared to the common Orpine found throughout New England, Tatarinow's stonecrop is much smaller and more compact, staying under a foot tall versus Orpine's 1-3 foot height.
Great Stonecrop is much larger and more robust than its close relative Orpine, with bigger leaves and flower clusters.
